passages.original: Μῦθος μέν, ὦ παῖ βασιλέως Ἀλεξάνδρου, Σύρων παλαιόν ἐστιν εὕρεμ᾿ ἀνθρώπων, οἳ πρίν ποτʼ ἦσαν ἐπὶ Νίνου τε καὶ Βήλου· πρῶτος δέ φασιν εἶπε παισὶν Ἑλλήνων Αἴσωπος ὁ σοφός, εἶπε καὶ Λιβυστίνοις λόγους Κυβίσσης. ἀλλʼ ἐγὼ νέῃ μούσῃ δίδωμι φαλάρῳ χρυσέῳ χαλινώσας τὸν μυθίαμβον ὥσπερ ἵππον ὁπλίτην. ὑπʼ ἐμοῦ δὲ πρώτου τῆς θύρας ἀνοιχθείσης εἰσῆλθον ἄλλοι, καὶ ψοφωτέρας μούσης γρίφοις ὁμοίας ἐκφέρουσι ποιήσεις, μαθόντες οὐδὲν πλεῖον ἢ γεγωνίσκειν.
passages.english: The fable, O son of King Alexander, is an ancient invention of the Syrians, men who lived long ago in the time of Ninus and Belus. The first, they say, to tell [fables] to the children of the Greeks was Aesop the wise, and Cybisses too told tales to the Libyans. But I give [it] to a new Muse, having bridled the fable-iambic with golden cheek-pieces like a warhorse. And when the door had been opened by me first, others came in, and they put out poems like riddles, of a more jangling Muse, having learned nothing more than to make themselves heard.
passages.notes: Verse (choliambics), the prologue to Book 2 of Babrius; rendered here as continuous prose because the edition gives no line divisions. 'Son of King Alexander': the addressee's identity is uncertain. 'Libystinois' (Libyans) and 'Kybissēs' (Cybisses) are as the text reads; Cybisses is otherwise obscure. 'phalaron' is a metal ornament on the bridle, possibly the cheek-pieces or a forehead boss. 'psophōteras' (more noisy, jangling) may imply empty or harsh sound. 'gegōniskein': to speak loudly, to make oneself heard.
